sources.entry: SimpleLogin - Open source email alias solution to protect your email address. Comes with browser extensions and mobile apps. (Source Code) MIT Docker/Python
SimpleLogin | Email alias service to protect your inbox

summary.one_liner: SimpleLogin is an open-source, self-hostable email alias service that forwards mail sent to aliases to your real inbox so your address stays private.
summary.what_it_does: The README is a self-hosting guide for running your own SimpleLogin instance on a Linux server using Docker containers. It covers DNS setup for MX, A, DKIM, SPF and DMARC records, and generating DKIM keys. It walks through installing and configuring Postfix against a Postgres database, which links relay domains and transport maps to the SimpleLogin email handler. It then describes running the webapp, email handler and job runner containers from the simplelogin/app:3.4.0 image, with an Nginx reverse proxy in front. The README notes that the API URL in the Chrome/Firefox extension and Android/iOS apps can be pointed at a self-hosted server. Options for disabling registration and making accounts premium are also described.
use_cases: hide my real email address from websites
forward alias emails to my inbox
run a private email alias server for my team
manage custom domains for email aliases
how_to_run: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y dnsutils
Create the sl/ data directories, generate DKIM keys with openssl, and set up MX, A, DKIM, SPF and DMARC DNS records
Install and configure Postfix with postfix-pgsql, then restart Postfix
Create simplelogin.env with your domain, FLASK_SECRET and database settings
Run flask db upgrade and python init_app.py using the simplelogin/app:3.4.0 Docker image
Start the sl-app, sl-email and sl-job-runner Docker containers, then set up Nginx and SSL
notable: Self-hosted alternative with a documented Docker-based setup using a Postgres container and a dedicated Docker network
Browser extensions and Android/iOS apps can be pointed at a self-hosted API URL
Includes DKIM, SPF and DMARC DNS configuration guidance for outbound mail
Splits the backend into webapp, email handler and job runner containers
Disables the alias suffix requirement for self-hosted installs
caveats: Requires a Linux server with at least 2 GB RAM recommended, open ports 25, 80, 443 and 22, and a domain you control for DNS
Setup is involved: Postfix, Postgres, DNS records, SSL and Nginx must all be configured manually
Accounts are not premium by default; unlimited aliases require a manual database update
